title: Sasarataicko (Sassakataka)
summary: Sasarataicko, also recorded as Sassakataka and Sakkatakka, appears in seventeenth-century records as an advisor involved in marking Cataconacke boundaries; Gaynell Stone later connected him with a Montaukett co-sachem recorded in 1702–1703.
content:
Sasarataicko, also recorded as Sassakataka and Sakkatakka, appears in seventeenth-century records connected with Wyandanch, Cataconacke, and later Montaukett land agreements. The spellings vary across colonial documents and later histories. This biography separates what the records say directly from Gaynell Stone’s later identification of the 1702–1703 signer with the earlier advisor.1

Cataconacke and boundary marking

John A. Strong describes Sasarataicko, or Sassakataka, as one of Wyandanch’s advisors during negotiations over Cataconacke, now associated with Old Field near Setauket, in 1659. A sworn deposition recorded on October 18, 1667 adds a more direct detail: Wyandanch appointed “Sakkatakka an Chekanno” to mark out the Cataconacke lands. The deposition calls Pauquatoun—not Sasarataicko—the former chief counselor to Wyandanch. Sasarataicko’s documented role in that testimony is boundary marking alongside Chekanno, or Cockenoe.2

A name in the 1663 succession record

A February 11, 1663/64 succession agreement says that Ponoqt, identified as the son of Sasagatacco, was to be regarded as a sachem while waiting his place in a regional line of succession. Stone connects Sasagatacco with Sassakataka and interprets the placement as evidence of a close relationship to Wyandanch’s leadership family. The document itself does not name the exact kinship between Sasagatacco and Wyandanch, so this biography does not assign one.3

The later co-sachem record

Stone identifies a signer written as Sassakatakow in September 1702 with the earlier advisor. The 1702 agreement concerned land-use rights east of Great Pond. A March 3, 1702/03 bond then names “Wiandance Sassakatoko, Indian Sachems, of Meantakett” in an agreement with East Hampton proprietors. These documents directly support the later signer’s Montaukett sachem status. Their identification with the person at Cataconacke is Stone’s historical reconstruction rather than an explicit statement in the original deeds, and is presented here with that limitation.4

A similar name kept separate

A 1681 whaling register includes the similar forms Sasaktakon and Sassakaton. The surviving entry does not securely identify that whaler as the earlier advisor or the later co-sachem. It is excluded from this biography rather than joined by spelling alone.5

Reading the map

The two map stops connect Cataconacke and the Montaukett homeland in record order. The line is a learning chronology, not a reconstruction of an exact route. The Montauk point is intentionally broad, and the connection to the 1702–1703 signer follows Stone’s published interpretation.

References

  • John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011), p. 51.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, vol. VI (1983), p. 59.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The History and Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), pp. 135, 184–185, 199, 324–327, 448, 452, and 455.
  • John A. Strong, America’s Early Whalemen (2018), p. 250.
why_this_matters: Sasarataicko's record shows Native governance through councils, boundary knowledge, succession, and negotiations over land—not only through a single famous leader. Reading the spelling variants carefully also shows why source transparency matters: later historians connect the early advisor and later co-sachem, but the original documents do not make every identity link explicit.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography and four linked Historic Moments distinguishing Sasarataicko's Cataconacke boundary role from later reconstructed identity links and a separate, uncertain whaling-register name.
